title: The assessment framework and functional unit

cards.question: What is meant by the value chain being the life cycle of a product?
cards.answer: The whole chain of stages from cradle (raw material extraction) to grave (disposal).
distractors: Only the manufacturing and sales stages
Only the use stage as experienced by the customer
The financial flow from supplier to retailer

cards.question: What do 'cradle to grave' mean in a life cycle perspective?
cards.answer: From raw material extraction (cradle) through manufacturing and use to disposal (grave).
distractors: From product design to product launch

cards.question: What are the four learning outcomes of the framework video?
cards.answer: Illustrate the generic life cycle of products and systems, explain the fundamentals of LCA, identify indicators for life cycle sustainability assessment, and formulate a simplified assessment approach.
distractors: Compute a carbon footprint, perform LCC, perform S-LCA and apply IPAT
Define SDGs, explain planetary boundaries, list EU regulations and design a taxonomy
Define the functional unit, build a Gantt chart, prepare a budget and write a report

cards.question: In the LCA picture, what are the technosphere and the ecosphere?
cards.answer: The technosphere is the human production system (activities); the ecosphere is the natural environment that supplies resources and receives emissions.
distractors: The technosphere is the natural environment; the ecosphere is the production system
Both denote the production system, at local and global scale
The technosphere is the use stage; the ecosphere is the disposal stage

cards.question: In LCA, what flows cross the boundary between the technosphere and the ecosphere?
cards.answer: Resources taken from the ecosphere and emissions released to it, which lead to impacts.

cards.question: What does the life cycle inventory table of substances (e.g. CO2, SO2, NOx, lead) represent?
cards.answer: Collected data on emissions (to air and water) from the product system, in grams per functional unit.
distractors: The legally allowed emission limits for a factory
A list of materials purchased by the customer

cards.question: What are the five elements of LCA listed in the lecture?
cards.answer: Define the goal of assessment, scope the system, collect data on emissions and resource use, translate emissions into environmental impacts, and interpret the results.
distractors: Define the budget, hire experts, collect samples, publish results and audit
Define the price, estimate the market, build the product, test it and sell it
Collect data, interpret it, translate it into policy, enforce it and report

cards.question: What does the goal definition step of LCA ask?
cards.answer: 'What is the question?'

cards.question: What is the last step of an LCA and what does it deliver?
cards.answer: Interpretation of results, giving the answer to the question.
distractors: Translation of emissions, giving the characterisation factors

cards.question: What is the difference between an inventory of emissions and an impact assessment in LCA?
cards.answer: The inventory quantifies emissions and resource use; the impact assessment translates them into environmental impacts.
distractors: The inventory defines the question; the impact assessment defines the system
The inventory is for social impacts; the impact assessment is for costs
There is no difference; they are two names for the same step

cards.question: What is the fundamental focus of LCA, as shown by comparing a disposable product with a reusable one?
cards.answer: The focus is on the service (function) delivered, so products are compared on delivering the same function.
distractors: The focus is on the product weight
The focus is on the production price
The focus is on the brand of the product

cards.question: Why does the lecture compare a single-use item with the same item used 30 times plus washing and transport?
cards.answer: To show that products must be compared on the same function, including all processes needed to deliver it, e.g. washing and transport.
distractors: To show that reusable products are always better
To show that washing has no environmental impact
To show that only production matters

cards.question: Is LCA mainly an absolute or a comparative method?
cards.answer: Comparative: it tells which alternative is better, not whether it is OK for the environment in an absolute sense.
distractors: Absolute: it tells whether the product is within planetary boundaries

cards.question: Why is 'is better than' not the same as 'is OK for the environment'?
cards.answer: A better alternative may still exceed what the environment can bear; that needs an absolute perspective.
distractors: Because absolute limits do not exist

cards.question: What is problem shifting, and how does LCA help avoid it?
cards.answer: Reducing one impact while increasing another or moving it to another stage; LCA avoids it through the full life cycle and all relevant impacts.
distractors: Moving production to another country; LCA prevents it by prohibiting transport
Shifting costs between stakeholders; LCA prevents it by pricing impacts
Shifting blame to consumers; LCA prevents it by labelling

cards.question: Which three features of LCA help avoid problem shifting?
cards.answer: The life cycle from cradle to grave, all relevant environmental impacts, and working environment and resource consumption (biotic and abiotic).
distractors: Only the use stage, only carbon and only costs
Only the supplier, only the customer and only the government
Local focus, single indicator and short time horizon

cards.question: What does LCSA stand for and what does it combine?
cards.answer: Life Cycle Sustainability Assessment, combining LCA, Life Cycle Costing (LCC) and Social LCA (S-LCA).
distractors: Life Cycle Systems Analysis, combining LCA, SDG and CE
Local Climate Sustainability Assessment, combining GHG, SDG and PB
Life Cycle Safety Audit, combining LCA, LCC and ISO

cards.question: What does LCC measure within LCSA?
cards.answer: The economic dimension: costs across the life cycle.

cards.question: What does S-LCA assess?
cards.answer: The social impacts of a product across its life cycle, following the UNEP guidelines.
distractors: The economic costs across the life cycle
The environmental impacts of a product
The market share of a product

cards.question: What is the difference between LCA and LCSA?
cards.answer: LCA covers environmental impacts only; LCSA additionally includes economic (LCC) and social (S-LCA) impacts.
distractors: LCA covers economy; LCSA covers environment
LCA is comparative; LCSA is absolute
LCA is qualitative; LCSA is quantitative

cards.question: Which UN body published the Guidelines for Social Life Cycle Assessment of Products and Organizations (2020)?
cards.answer: UNEP, the United Nations Environment Programme.
distractors: UNDP, the United Nations Development Programme

cards.question: Does this course apply full LCSA?
cards.answer: No; it aims to cover all aspects in a life cycle perspective through a simplified approach.
distractors: Yes, students must perform full LCSA

cards.question: What does the MECO framework stand for?
cards.answer: Materials, Energy, Chemicals and Others: the causes of environmental impact.

cards.question: In the MECO framework, what does the 'Materials' driver contribute to?
cards.answer: Depletion of natural resources.

cards.question: In the MECO framework, what impacts does 'Energy' drive?
cards.answer: Climate change, acidification, photochemical ozone formation, etc.

cards.question: In the MECO framework, what impacts does 'Chemicals' drive?
cards.answer: Human and ecological toxicity and ozone depletion.

cards.question: In the MECO framework, what are examples of 'Others'?
cards.answer: Land use, water use, social impacts, etc.

cards.question: Which life cycle stages does the MECO framework cross with the causes of environmental impact?
cards.answer: Extraction of raw materials, manufacturing stage, use stage and disposal stage.

cards.question: In the Quantitative Sustainability framework, which five impact areas are listed?
cards.answer: Resources, environment, economic, social/health and transition.
distractors: Climate, water, soil, air and noise
Production, use, disposal, transport and storage
Society, economy, environment, technology and policy

cards.question: How is the resources impact area measured in the framework?
cards.answer: By use of biotic and abiotic resources, and circular economy indicators.
distractors: By carbon footprint and absolute boundaries

cards.question: How is the environment impact area measured in the framework?
cards.answer: By climate change (carbon footprint) and absolute boundaries.
distractors: By use of biotic and abiotic resources

cards.question: How is the economic impact area measured in the framework?
cards.answer: By costs.

cards.question: How is the social/health impact area measured in the framework?
cards.answer: By socioeconomic impacts and health impacts.

cards.question: How is the transition impact area assessed in the framework?
cards.answer: By qualitative or semiquantitative assessment.

cards.question: What is the difference between the MECO framework and the Quantitative Sustainability framework?
cards.answer: MECO links causes (materials, energy, chemicals, others) to environmental impacts; the Quantitative Sustainability framework crosses sustainability impact areas with life cycle stages and indicators.
distractors: MECO covers economic and social impacts; the Quantitative framework covers only environment
MECO is absolute; the Quantitative framework is comparative
They are the same framework under different names

cards.question: What are the four summary points of the framework video?
cards.answer: LCA is comparative and covers a life cycle; the object of assessment must be precisely defined; LCSA adds economic and social impacts; the course uses a simplified approach.
distractors: LCA is absolute; define the budget; LCSA replaces LCA; the course uses full LCSA
LCA is qualitative; skip the object definition; LCSA is optional; the course uses only carbon
LCA is only for products; ignore use; LCSA is legal; the course uses SDGs only

cards.question: Why must the object of assessment be defined precisely?
cards.answer: It is needed to make a quantitative assessment and crucial for comparative assessments.
distractors: It is needed only for legal reasons
It is needed only for the report layout
It is not needed if the product is well known

cards.question: What is the object of assessment defined through?
cards.answer: The function it provides: the functional unit.

cards.question: Which questions does the use context ask when defining a product or system?
cards.answer: What it should be used for, what it does, for whom, how long and how often, and where in the world.
distractors: Who built it, when, how cheaply and with what profit
How heavy, how colourful, how big and how new
Which legal entity, which patent, which supplier and which price

cards.question: What value does the use context focus on?
cards.answer: The value contribution the product delivers to the user.

cards.question: What are obligatory properties of a product?
cards.answer: Properties decisive for customers perceiving it as that product, possible legal requirements, and properties that help define the product.
distractors: Properties that make the product attractive compared to competitors
Properties that only apply in the use stage

cards.question: What are positioning properties of a product?
cards.answer: Properties that make the product attractive and position it relative to comparable products.
distractors: Properties that define the product category

cards.question: What is the difference between obligatory and positioning properties?
cards.answer: Obligatory properties define the product and are decisive for perceiving it as such; positioning properties differentiate it from comparable products.
distractors: Obligatory properties are optional extras; positioning properties are legal
Obligatory properties apply to cost; positioning properties apply to impact
Obligatory properties are in the use stage; positioning properties in disposal

cards.question: Which properties does the functional unit take its point of origin in?
cards.answer: The key obligatory property.

cards.question: What does the functional unit express?
cards.answer: The service the product/system delivers in quantitative and qualitative terms: quantity, duration and central qualities.
distractors: The weight of the product only
The list of materials in the product

cards.question: What is the role of the functional unit in comparative studies?
cards.answer: It ensures equivalence between the compared services/systems.

cards.question: Which dimensions are included in a functional unit definition?
cards.answer: What, how much, how well, how long (how many times) and where.
distractors: Who, when, which brand, which colour and how expensive
Input, output, cost, waste and revenue
Materials, energy, chemicals, others and time

cards.question: What is a functional unit of a water boiler given in the lecture?
cards.answer: Heat 1 litre of water to the boiling point three times a day for a year in Denmark.
distractors: Own one water boiler for a year
Consume 1 kWh of electricity per day

cards.question: In the water boiler example, which part of the FU states 'how much'?
cards.answer: 1 litre of water.

cards.question: In the water boiler example, which part of the FU states 'how well'?
cards.answer: To the boiling point.

cards.question: In the water boiler example, which part of the FU states 'how long'?
cards.answer: Three times a day for a year.

cards.question: What is a reference flow?
cards.answer: The measure of outputs from processes in a given product system required to fulfil the function expressed by the functional unit (ISO 14044).
distractors: The flow of money through the supply chain
The flow of emissions to the ecosphere
The flow of waste in disposal

cards.question: What is the difference between the functional unit and the reference flow?
cards.answer: The functional unit expresses the function delivered; the reference flow is the amount of product needed to deliver it.
distractors: The functional unit is the amount of product; the reference flow is the function
The functional unit is for costs; the reference flow is for emissions

cards.question: In the paint example, what is the reference flow for paint A and paint B?
cards.answer: 0.67 L of water-based paint A and 0.15 L of water-based paint B.
distractors: 0.15 L of paint A and 0.67 L of paint B

cards.question: Why does the paint example have different reference flows for paint A and B?
cards.answer: Because the paints differ in performance: A needs two applications and a re-paint every 2½ years; B needs one application and lasts 5 years.
distractors: Because they come from different suppliers

cards.question: What is a suitable functional unit of a car, according to the lecture?
cards.answer: Transporting 1 passenger safely/comfortably over 1 km commuting in Europe.

cards.question: What is the reference flow of the car functional unit?
cards.answer: 1 person-km (pers-km), or kg-km when cargo mass is transported.

cards.question: Which are obligatory properties of a car?
cards.answer: Transporting passengers and cargo, being safe, and fulfilling legislative requirements.
distractors: Number of seats, motor size and acceleration

cards.question: Which are positioning properties of a car?
cards.answer: Number of seats and size, motor size and acceleration, design and luxury features.

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a car include the amount of kilometres driven?
cards.answer: Yes, it is part of 'how much'.
distractors: No, it is a design property
No, it is only part of the use stage
No, it is only a legal requirement

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a car include the number of passengers?
cards.answer: Yes, it is part of what is delivered (passenger transport).
distractors: No, because it is a positioning property of the car size
No, because it is only an emission factor
No, because it is part of disposal

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a car include the car's size or fuel efficiency?
cards.answer: No; size and efficiency are product properties (positioning or performance), not the function.

cards.question: What is a suitable functional unit of a coffee, according to the lecture?
cards.answer: Serving 1 dl of hot coffee once in Denmark.

cards.question: What is the reference flow of the coffee functional unit?
cards.answer: 1 dl of coffee.

cards.question: What are the obligatory properties of a coffee?
cards.answer: Hot, aroma intensity and flavour that distinguish it as coffee, and served in a drinking device.

cards.question: What are positioning properties of a coffee?
cards.answer: Roasting profile, aroma/flavour type, caffeine content, brewing method.

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a coffee include the amount of coffee served?
cards.answer: Yes, it is part of 'how much'.
distractors: No, it is only a positioning property
No, it is only a cost
No, it is part of disposal

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a coffee include the number of times the coffee is served?
cards.answer: Yes, it is 'how long/how many times'.
distractors: No, it concerns only the brewing
No, only the first serving counts
No, it is part of the reference flow

cards.question: Does the functional unit of a coffee include brewing method or electricity used for brewing?
cards.answer: No; these are positioning properties or part of the system's inputs, not the function.

cards.question: What does a process tree show for an EV (electric vehicle) life cycle?
cards.answer: The stages from raw materials extraction, manufacturing, transportation and use to end of life, with processes in each.

cards.question: What are the five stages shown in the EV process flowchart?
cards.answer: Raw materials extraction, manufacturing processes, transportation and distribution, use stage, and end of life.
distractors: Design, prototype, test, launch and support
Mining, smelting, casting, painting and selling
Purchase, registration, use, repair and scrapping

cards.question: Which raw materials are listed for an EV?
cards.answer: Lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, steel, aluminium, plastics and glass.

cards.question: What happens to the battery in the EV end of life stage?
cards.answer: It may be reused in second life (grid storage) or material recycled (hydrometallurgy).
distractors: It is returned to the mine

cards.question: Which processes belong to the use stage of an EV?
cards.answer: Grid electricity consumption, routine maintenance and software updates, and replacement of consumables (tires, wipers, fluids).

cards.question: What is the goal of the qualitative assessment exercise in the teaching session?
cards.answer: To identify which life cycle stages are most important for each type of impact (resources, environment, economy, social) and why.
distractors: To compute the carbon footprint of a coffee
To define the functional unit of a car
To calculate the reference flow of paint

cards.question: What is the IPAT equation?
cards.answer: I = P × A × T: impact equals population times affluence times technology.

cards.question: What does I stand for in IPAT?
cards.answer: The environmental impact.

cards.question: What do P, A and T stand for in IPAT?
cards.answer: P is population, A is affluence (GDP per person) and T is technology (impact per unit of GDP).
distractors: P is production, A is activity and T is time
P is pollution, A is area and T is temperature
P is price, A is availability and T is transport

cards.question: How is IPAT written using GDP?
cards.answer: I = Pop × (GDP/person) × (I/GDP).

cards.question: What does the affluence factor (GDP per person) represent?
cards.answer: The material standard of living.
distractors: The environmental impact per created value
The size of the global population

cards.question: What does the technology factor (I/GDP) represent?
cards.answer: The environmental impact per created value.

cards.question: Who introduced the IPAT relationship?
cards.answer: Ehrlich and Holdren (1971), with Commoner (1972).

cards.question: In the IPAT projection, how much will population and affluence each grow in 50 years?
cards.answer: Each to about 200% of today's value.

cards.question: What does the IPAT projection conclude about P·A in 50 years?
cards.answer: Total human demand/consumption will grow by at least a factor of 4–5.

cards.question: What happens to total environmental impact in 50 years if the technology factor remains unchanged?
cards.answer: It grows accordingly, by the same factor as P·A.

cards.question: By what factor must the technology factor T be reduced to achieve environmental sustainability?
cards.answer: A factor of 4 to 20.
distractors: It does not need to be reduced

cards.question: What are the take-aways of the IPAT video?
cards.answer: Global environmental impact is driven by human consumption and demand; technology can reduce impact (4–20 times more efficient), but consumption itself must also be addressed.
distractors: Technology alone will solve the problem; consumption is irrelevant
Population is the only driver; technology is irrelevant

cards.question: What is the rebound effect?
cards.answer: Efficiency gains are partly or fully offset by increased consumption, so total demand and impact may not fall.
distractors: Impacts bounce back after a recession
A product returns to the market after being recalled

cards.question: Why is the rebound effect relevant to IPAT?
cards.answer: Because improved technology (lower T) can raise consumption (higher A), undermining the reduction.
distractors: Because it increases the technology factor

cards.question: What is the difference between addressing the technology factor and addressing consumption?
cards.answer: The technology factor reduces impact per unit of value created; addressing consumption reduces the amount of demand itself.
distractors: Technology reduces population; consumption reduces affluence
Technology addresses costs; consumption addresses emissions
They are two names for the same measure
